items.title: 7 mind-bending comparisons between the Universe and the human body
items.summary: Our observable Universe is enormous compared to a human: over 10²⁶ times as large. This horizontally-oriented logarithmic map of the Universe shows how, from left-to-right, we go from Earth-sized scales to the largest cosmic distances of all. As spectacular as this logarithmic view is, it “only” spans about 20 orders of magnitude: from the size of the Earth to the size of the present-day cosmic horizon. A human is a further factor of 7,000,000 smaller in scale, roughly, than planet Earth. ( Credit : Pablo Carlos Budassi) These 7 comparisons give perspective to these vastly different scales. The elements of the periodic table, and where they originate, are detailed in this image above. While most elements originate primarily in supernovae or merging neutron stars, many vitally important elements are created, in part or even mostly, in planetary nebulae, which do not arise from the first generation of stars. Beryllium, boron, and some lithium are primarily created through a process known as spallation: when cosmic rays strike and split apart heavier atomic nuclei. The human body, although it contains over 70 types of atoms, is primarily made up of only four: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen. Credit : NASA/CXC/SAO/K. Divona 1.) Human cells equal galactic planetary bodies . There are approximately 30-40 trillion red blood cells in the human body: by far the most common type of cell that is made by humans within the body, and representing around 90% of all cells. In addition, approximately an equal number of non-native cells live within our microbiome, mostly inside our digestive tract. Credit: Design Cells / Adobe Stock Each human body possesses 80 trillion cells, half of which are human . While cells in the digestive tract and red blood cells make up the majority of cells in the human body, the next most common cell type are the cells of the immune system, making up approximately 1.8 trillion cells on their own. Their estimated distribution and location is shown here. Credit : Ron Sender/BioRender.com Our galaxy contains 400 billion stars, with around 100 rounded objects per stellar system . Although Earth and Venus are the two largest rocky objects in the Solar System, Mars, Mercury, as well as over 100 of the largest moons, asteroids, and Kuiper belt objects have all achieved hydrostatic equilibrium. Ganymede and Titan are larger than Mercury, but Callisto, at 99% of Mercury’s size, has just one-third of Mercury’s mass. All told, all known objects with diameters greater than 800 km are in hydrostatic equilibrium. The number of rounded bodies is expected to be similar among nearly all star systems. Credit : Emily Lakdawalla. Data from NASA / JPL, JHUAPL/SwRI, SSI, and UCLA / MPS / DLR / IDA, processed by Gordan Ugarkovic, Ted Stryk, Bjorn Jonsson, Roman Tkachenko, and Emily Lakdawalla 2.) More cells than overall galaxies . Only approximately 1000 stars, totaling ~175 solar masses, are present in the entirety of dwarf galaxies Segue 1 and Segue 3, the latter of which has a gravitational mass of an impressive 600,000 Suns. The stars making up the dwarf satellite Segue 1 are circled here. As we discover smaller, fainter galaxies with fewer numbers of stars, we begin to recognize just how common these small galaxies are as well as how elevated their dark matter-to-normal matter ratios can be; there may be as many as 100 for every galaxy similar to the Milky Way, with dark matter outmassing normal matter by factors of many hundreds or even more. Credit : Marla Geha/Keck Observatory This outstrips the number of galaxies in the observable Universe: estimated at 20 trillion . This diagram shows the phases of apoptotic cell clearance. Apoptosis is the process by which the body regularly destroys older cells, paving the way for newer, healthy, less damaged cells to take their place. Every day, somewhere around 50-70 billion cells die inside your body. Credit : I.K.H. Poon et al., Nature Reviews Immunology, 2014 3.) Daily cell death comprises a whole galaxy of stars . The spiral galaxy Messier 33, shown as imaged by an amateur astronomer with X-ray data from NASA’s Chandra overlaid in pink, is also known as the Triangulum galaxy: a faint galaxy visible in the southern skies. First recorded in 1654, it is the faintest object visible by typical, unaided human eyes at a distance of 2.878 million light-years: several hundred million light-years more distant than Andromeda. As the Local Group’s third largest galaxy, it contains an estimated 40-50 billion stars. Credit : Optical: Warren Keller; X-ray: NASA/CXC/SAO/P. Plucinsky et al. Each day, 50-70 billion cells die : comparable to our total number of brain neurons . The brain is a network of neurons, connected by synapses, embedded in a substrate of four different types of glial cells. There is both white and gray matter in the brain, and a three-layer protective casing surrounding it, all fed by blood vessels. A typical human brain contains an estimated 86 billion neurons. How this organ produces consciousness remains highly mysterious. Credit: Dr_Microbe / Adobe Stock 4.) A galaxy cluster’s galaxies are like organs, muscles, and bones . Most of the largest known galaxies in the Universe are found at the hearts of massive galaxy clusters, like the nearby galaxy cluster shown here. While the largest and most massive galaxy clusters possess several thousand galaxies, they are rare. More typically, galaxy clusters contain a few hundred galaxies, with an “average” galaxy cluster possessing right around 1000 significant galactic members. Credit : CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA; Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska, Anchorage/NSF’s NOIRLab), Jen Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF’s NOIRLab), Mahdi Zamani & Davide de Martin (NSF’s NOIRLab) Most galaxy clusters have around 1000 galaxies . This view of the human body, both shallow as well as posterior and anterior, shows the major muscle groups found inside the human body. Along with 79 organs and 206 bones, there are over 600 and closer to 700 identified skeletal muscles within the human body. These three systems, combined make up the majority of a human body’s mass. Credit : OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology/Wikimedia Commons Meanwhile, humans have 79 organs, 206 bones, and 700 skeletal muscles . Although human beings are made of cells, at a more fundamental level, we’re made of atoms. All told, there are close to ~10^28 atoms in a human body, mostly hydrogen by number but mostly oxygen (due to water) and carbon (due to the musculoskeletal system and our organs) by mass. Credit : Dave Collins/Dave’s Brain 5.) Water is the body’s “dark matter.” Human bodies gradually evolve in terms of their water-weight content over the course of their lifetime. A zygote’s mass is nearly 100% water, a developing fetus is around 90%, a newborn baby’s water content is 75-80%, which decreases to around 70% in childhood, 55-65% in adulthood and down to about 50% in the elderly. Credit: Kati Finell / Adobe Stock Humans are mostly (50-80%) water , while dark matter dominates (80-85%) the cosmos’s mass. items.title: I Thought I Was Good at Something
items.summary: and then I lose an hour to those billiard-trick-shot videos, magnificent, their impossible spins, flawless timing, the punctuated clunk of the corner pockets like God exhaling just a little. I lose another hour watching and another. Months evaporate this way. There’s the one where the cue ball kisses every single solid in procession as if in a receiving line before sinking the eight. There’s the simple shot, a spin so hard, the cue circles back on itself only a few inches away to sink a ball exactly behind it. If I eat I don’t remember having done so. If I have lovers they haven’t called. If I have a name I will need you to remind me. But then it’s today and something snaps in me like a glowstick, bright and temporary. My mother phones and starts talking about identifying possum tracks in the snow. Isn’t it summer? I think and venture out in the city. I get on the train, head to whatever job I recall having had but still the world is here too much and like an eclipse it’s bad for you to look at directly, the naked tenderness of the men reading self-help books on the train—all their failures and desires written right there on the covers. I surface to the streets of this city made crazy with commuters, how perfect we are, moving toward what it is we chase. How one by one we drop into the manholes on the corners with a clunk.

items.title: Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI
items.summary: B ecause literary journals tend to have small circulations, few readers are likely to have come across “ The Whistleblower ,” a short story by the Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza. Published in 2021 in a journal called Transition , the story is a taut and closely observed political thriller in miniature. Its narrator, a sharp but inexperienced computer-science graduate in Harare, Zimbabwe, encounters an intelligence officer at the mall—a former teacher of his—who now wants something from him. At first, the graduate is nervous for what turns out to be the wrong reason: “I’d had a brief relationship with his niece Agatha and I wasn’t sure whether he knew about this or how he felt about it if he did.” A more recent story with Kundizeza’s name on it, “ The Blue Fighter ,” will surely find its way to more readers. Last week, it was named the winner of the prestigious Caine Prize for African Writing, which awards 10,000 British pounds (about $13,000) for a short story by an African writer. Some previous winners, including Namwali Serpell and NoViolet Bulawayo , are now among the world’s most celebrated authors. Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad—maudlin and full of tired tropes. Here, the Zimbabwean narrator is the son of a hapless father who squanders the family’s money trying to breed fish in tanks, to the mother’s chagrin. “‘We can’t afford this house anymore,’ she said one evening, placing the notice in front of him while he tested the seal on his newest creation,” the story reads. “Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come.” At the end, the narrator compares the last remaining fish to his family: “Not broken, just learning how to live differently. Alone, sometimes. But still moving. Still here.” That this narrator has all the personality of a chatbot is probably not coincidental. The AI detector Pangram flags almost the entire story as AI-generated; a notable exception is its epigraph, also about a father with a fish fixation, which is excerpted from what’s described as an unpublished poem by Vangile Gantsho. This isn’t the first prize-winning story to be flagged by Pangram. It comes after similar scandals over this year’s Commonwealth Prize and Prix Goncourt —two other renowned literature contests—in which Pangram flagged AI use among finalists. In the case of the Commonwealth Prize, one of them eventually won ; the Prix Goncourt pulled a writer from consideration after suspected AI use was compounded by plagiarism allegations over his earlier work. Any of these incidents might have been written off as a fluke. Together, they point to something of a crisis of trust—in both writers and technology—that threatens to undermine a global system of literary recognition. [ Read: The literary AI scandal that changes everything ] AI detection is fallible , which has raised concerns among some readers and writers about the prospect of false positives. But Pangram, which uses AI for its classification of text, is highly accurate : The company says its tool mistakenly labels human text as AI in about one in 24,000 cases; outside research also finds false positives to be extremely rare. When I ran all 25 of the previous Caine Prize-winning stories through Pangram, it labeled them as 100 percent human-written; the same is true of Kundizeza’s “The Whistleblower.” I reached out to Kundizeza about Pangram’s assessment of “The Blue Fighter” through his agent, Adrienne Ingrum at the Serendipity Literary Agency. She wrote that Regina Brooks, the agency’s CEO, would send me “evidence that the author and we at Serendipity are completely confident that the story is Simba’s own work.” Neither Ingrum nor Brooks followed up before publication. I also spoke at length with Ellah Wakatama, who chairs the Caine Prize’s board of trustees. Wakatama, a longtime book editor, told me that AI-generated fiction is not eligible for the prize. As soon as she learned of an inquiry I’d sent about the Pangram assessment of Kundizeza’s story, she and her colleagues initiated an investigation and contacted the author. Wakatama told me that she and a colleague will interview the prize judges, and that she’ll reread Kundizeza’s story and talk with him in detail about his methods. She added that a colleague has been in contact with Kundizeza’s agent about whether a verification process might include, say, reviewing previous drafts. Yet Wakatama forcefully rejected the notion that an AI detector could, or should, be used to gauge AI involvement. “My stance, as the person who leads the prize, is that if there is such an accusation, I want proof that does not come from a machine.” She said she planned to approach Kundizeza with “compassion” and the presumption of honesty. Wakatama is also Zimbabwean. “As an African,” she said, “my first stance is, if I ask you, Are you telling the truth? and if you say yes, I am going to believe you—especially because the accusers are not coming from amongst our own people.” Wakatama remarked on details in Kundizeza’s story that strike her as so typically Zimbabwean that a Zimbabwean must have written them: the shame of moving from a nice suburb to a less privileged township; how the mother’s initial forbearance with the father gives way to taking matters into her own hands. Wakatama also perceives multiple layers of meaning. She doesn’t think AI models are capable of that kind of cultural or literary nuance. [ Read: The Pangram backlash unfolding on college campuses ] But then, she acknowledged that she doesn’t use AI or AI detectors. “My first response when somebody asks me to use AI is that I think about water and energy,” she said—that is, AI companies’ excessive use of both. “That honestly overwhelms me, and I don’t want to.” Wakatama isn’t involved in choosing the Caine Prize winner—a panel of judges reads all the submissions—but her approach to AI is common among organizations that award prizes or other honors to writers. Partly, this is a pragmatic response to the risk of false positives. “Our legal parameters don’t allow us to contest the honesty of our writers just because a tool says that,” Razmi Farook, the director-general of the Commonwealth Foundation, told me during the scandal over its prize. But this wariness also reflects a general aversion, in literary and arts circles, to engaging with AI products, even if just to understand them better—including Pangram. The start-up’s product itself is based on AI, and it belongs to the Silicon Valley ecosystem; the company recently raised $50 million in funding, according to a person familiar with the deal. The skepticism is easy to understand, but it might be shortsighted. Research suggests that the people most familiar with AI output excel at sniffing it out. I’ve covered AI for almost a decade, and have written fiction for even longer; in short, I’ve had plenty of exposure to both literature and chatbot output. I know from experience that, for example, AI models aren’t terrible at picking up on cultural details. When I read “The Blue Fighter,” I was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions ; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms. “Anger burns out eventually,” the narrator’s mother says at one point. “Hunger doesn’t.” The earlier story by Kundizeza lacked those stylistic qualities, its prose and dialogue far more plainspoken and natural-sounding: “So how are things with my niece, huh?” the intelligence officer asks at one point. What I also noticed, more disturbingly, was the presence of stereotypes about African life common among outsiders: a blundering, unemployed father; a resilient matriarch who dispenses clichéd approximations of wisdom; an environment of deprivation.
